lessons.title: My Neighbourhood
objectives: Name places in the neighbourhood
Describe places as near or far
prerequisites: Can talk about places they visit
explanation: A neighbourhood is the area around your home. It has places like shops, a park, a school, a hospital, places of worship, a bus stop and other people's homes.
Some places are near (a short walk away), and some are far (you need a bus or car).
Knowing your neighbourhood helps you find your way and feel safe.

story.title: Zuri's Walk to the Park
story.text: Zuri walked to the park with her father. They passed the vegetable shop, the post office and a big blue gate. "That gate is a landmark," said Papa. "If you see it, the park is near." Zuri counted: vegetable shop, post office, blue gate, park! Now she knew the way.

lessons.title: Seeing Like a Bird
objectives: Understand that a map shows a place from above

explanation: A bird flying above sees the tops of things: the roof of a house, the round top of a tree, the flat top of a table. A map is like a picture drawn from above.
On a map, we use simple shapes and symbols: a square for a table, a circle for a rug, a little tree shape for a tree.
Maps help us find things and plan where to go.

A treasure map shows where treasure is hidden.

story.text: Mayur the peacock flew up high above the village. "Everything looks different!" Houses were squares, the pond was a blue circle, the road a grey ribbon. Mayur drew what he saw and gave it to Kiko. "A map!" said Kiko. "Now I can find the pond."

objectives: Give and follow directions using left, right, forward and turn

explanation: Directions help us move from one place to another. Forward means go straight ahead. Turn left or turn right changes which way we face.
A route is the path we take. We can describe it in steps: "Go forward 5 steps, turn left, go forward 3 steps."
Landmarks make directions easier: "Turn right at the big tree."

lessons.title: Spinning the Globe
objectives: Explain that a globe is a model of the round Earth
Identify land and water on a globe
prerequisites: Knows maps show places from above
explanation: The Earth is round like a ball. A globe is a small model of the Earth that we can hold and spin.
On a globe, blue shows water — oceans and seas. Green, brown and yellow show land. There is much more water than land on Earth!
A map is flat, but a globe is round, so a globe shows the true shape of the Earth best.

story.text: Nova showed Kiko a photo of Earth taken from space. "It's mostly blue!" said Kiko. "That's the ocean," said Nova. She spun a globe and stopped it with her finger. "And this is India — our home, on this big blue ball."

lessons.title: Never Eat Soggy Wheat
objectives: Name the four cardinal directions
Use a compass rose to describe locations on a map
prerequisites: Gives directions with left and right
explanation: There are four main (cardinal) directions: north, east, south and west. A memory trick going clockwise: "Never Eat Soggy Wheat" (N, E, S, W).
The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. A magnetic compass needle points towards magnetic north.
Maps have a compass rose showing directions. Usually north is at the top. We can say "The Himalayas are in the north of India; Kanyakumari is in the south."

a symbol on a map showing directions

lessons.title: States and Neighbours
objectives: Locate several Indian states and their capitals
Name India's neighbouring countries
explanation: India is divided into 28 states and 8 union territories. Each state has a capital: Maharashtra — Mumbai, Tamil Nadu — Chennai, West Bengal — Kolkata, Karnataka — Bengaluru. New Delhi is India's capital.
India's neighbours include Pakistan to the west, China and Nepal and Bhutan to the north, Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east, and Sri Lanka and the Maldives across the sea to the south.
An atlas is a book of maps. Using its index and grid helps us find places.

context.text: As of 2019 reorganisation, India has 28 states and 8 union territories; administrative divisions can change by law.

lessons.title: Seven Continents, Five Oceans
objectives: Name and locate the seven continents and five oceans
Describe the hemispheres
prerequisites: Knows land and water on a globe
explanation: Earth's land is divided into seven continents: Asia (the largest, where India is), Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia (Oceania).
The five oceans are the Pacific (the largest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. India is in the Northern Hemisphere. Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons are opposite to ours.

units.title: Map Scale and Distance

lessons.title: How Far Is It?
objectives: Use a scale bar to calculate real distances
Compare large-scale and small-scale maps
explanation: Maps are much smaller than the real world. A scale tells us how much smaller: "1 cm = 10 km" means every centimetre on the map stands for 10 kilometres in real life.
To find a distance: measure on the map with a ruler, then multiply by the scale. 4 cm on a 1 cm = 10 km map is 40 km.
A large-scale map shows a small area in lots of detail (a neighbourhood). A small-scale map shows a large area with less detail (the whole world).

vocabulary.meaning: how map distance relates to real distance
a line on a map showing distances
shows a small area in detail
shows a large area with less detail

examples: A city map shows individual streets.
A world map shows only big cities.

story.title: The Trip Planner
story.text: Zuri's family planned a road trip. On the map, the next town was 6 cm away. The scale said 1 cm = 25 km. "That's 150 km," Zuri calculated. "At 50 km an hour, about 3 hours." Her father was impressed. "You're our navigator now!"

lessons.title: Earth's Grid
objectives: Read latitude and longitude coordinates
Locate places using coordinates
explanation: Latitude lines run east–west around the Earth and measure how far north or south a place is from the equator (0°), up to 90° at the poles.
Longitude lines run from pole to pole and measure how far east or west a place is from the Prime Meridian (0°) through Greenwich, London, up to 180°.
Together they give coordinates. New Delhi is at about 28.6° N, 77.2° E. The Tropic of Cancer (about 23.4° N) passes through the middle of India.

vocabulary.meaning: distance north or south of the equator in degrees
distance east or west of the Prime Meridian in degrees
0° longitude
a pair of numbers giving a location

examples: Mumbai: about 19° N, 73° E.
GPS on phones uses latitude and longitude.

story.title: The Ship's Navigator
story.text: Centuries ago, sailors could find latitude by measuring the height of the Sun or Pole Star, but longitude was much harder. In the 1700s, John Harrison built accurate sea clocks; by comparing local time with home time, sailors could finally work out longitude and stop getting lost.

lessons.title: What Time Is It There?
objectives: Explain why time zones exist
Calculate times in other zones
explanation: Because the Earth rotates, it's day in some places and night in others. To keep noon roughly when the Sun is highest, the world is divided into time zones, usually one hour apart (about every 15° of longitude).

India uses one time zone: Indian Standard Time (IST), which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+5:30). When it's 12:00 noon in India, it's 6:30 am in London (UTC) in winter.
Climate zones depend on latitude and other factors: tropical near the equator, dry deserts, temperate in mid-latitudes, polar near the poles, and highland in mountains.

context.text: IST is based on the 82.5° E meridian near Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh. Some people propose two time zones for India because the Sun rises much earlier in the northeast than in the west.

vocabulary.meaning: a region using the same standard time
Indian Standard Time, UTC+5:30
Coordinated Universal Time
where the calendar date changes, near 180°

examples: A video call to a cousin in the USA must account for time differences.
The sun rises over an hour earlier in Arunachal Pradesh than in Gujarat.

story.title: The Midnight Birthday Call
story.text: Riya wanted to wish her uncle in California a happy birthday at exactly midnight his time. In summer, California was 12 and a half hours behind India. She did the maths and set an alarm for 12:30 pm the next day in India. Her uncle laughed: "Right on time!"

lessons.title: Push and Pull
objectives: Explain population distribution and density
Analyse migration using push and pull factors
explanation: Population density is the number of people per square kilometre. Some areas, like the Gangetic Plain, are very densely populated because of fertile land and water; others, like the Thar Desert or high Himalayas, are sparse.
People migrate for many reasons. Push factors make people leave (lack of jobs, drought, conflict); pull factors attract them (jobs, education, safety, family).
India is urbanising: a growing share of people live in cities. Cities offer opportunities but face challenges of housing, transport, water and pollution.

context.text: Census data show India's urban population share rising from about 17% in 1951 to about 31% in 2011.

vocabulary.meaning: people per square kilometre
moving from one place to another to live
a reason to leave a place
a reason to move to a place
the growth of cities

examples: A farmer moving to a city after crop failure (push) for construction work (pull).
Students moving to cities for universities.

story.title: Two Brothers
story.text: Two brothers grew up in a village in Bihar. When the monsoon failed twice, one moved to Mumbai for construction work and sent money home. The other stayed and started a small dairy with a loan. Their lives showed both sides of migration — opportunity, hardship and connection between village and city.

lessons.title: Layers of Information
objectives: Explain GPS, remote sensing and GIS
Describe uses of geospatial technology
explanation: GPS uses signals from satellites to find a receiver's location. India has its own regional system, NavIC.

Remote sensing means gathering information about Earth from a distance, usually satellites. Images can show forest cover, floods, crop health and city growth. ISRO's satellites provide such data, and platforms like Bhuvan share it.
A Geographic Information System (GIS) combines layers of data on a map — roads, rivers, population, schools — to answer questions: Where should a new hospital go? Which villages are at flood risk?

context.text: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is ISRO's regional satellite navigation system; Bhuvan is ISRO's geoportal.

vocabulary.meaning: satellite system for finding location
collecting data about Earth from a distance

one set of mapped information

examples: Flood maps from satellite images guiding rescue teams.
Delivery apps using GPS to track riders.

story.title: Mapping the Flood
story.text: During a severe flood, satellite images showed which areas were underwater. GIS analysts overlaid layers of population, roads and hospitals. Rescue teams knew which villages to reach first and which roads were still usable. "Maps," said one officer, "saved lives today."
